To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there are significant and substantial disparities in blood pressure control between health systems, and within systems across different clinical sites, that are not fully explained by individual patient characteristics.

after controlling for standard individual factors, substantial differences in hypertension rates remained between health systems and were associated with differences in local quality improvement programs and disparities across health systems.
we found significant differences in hypertension control between 3 health systems, even after accounting for differences between patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the development of a data-sharing collaborative among health systems, and how this collaboration could lead to improved hypertension outcomes.
the development of a data sharing infrastructure for a multi-institutional collaborative research network.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data presented in the manuscript suggest that there are significant and substantial differences between health systems, even when controlling for standard predictors of hypertension control.
there were significant disparities in the control of blood pressure between health systems and within health systems.
the results of this study demonstrate that there are disparities in blood pressure control between health care systems and within health care systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found significant differences in hypertension control among three health systems participating in a regional data-sharing collaboration.
there are disparities in hypertension control among patients with hypertension, even when controlling for individual patient characteristics.
there are differences in the quality of blood pressure management across and within health systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we were able to use the common data repository and standardized definitions to compare hypertension control across three health systems.

we can identify disparities across systems and within systems, and that these disparities are not due to the usual suspects, such as age, gender, or race, but rather due to the usual suspect: the health system.
we can use the data we have to identify and address these disparities, and to do this we need to work together.
